title: The Fourth Patriarch: Guarding the One Without Moving
author: Annotated by Zhanran
excerpt: The following is the instruction on “guarding the one without moving” by the Fourth Patriarch of the Chan school, Master Daoxin, in the Essential Expedient Method for Entering the Way and Settling the Mind. Its method is simple, concrete, practical, and safe (it will not go astray); it is the fundamental practice for entering the Way — unify the mind in one place, and nothing is not accomplished.

inline.s: Gaze upon one object, keeping the mind fixed without confusion;
If the mind scatters, immediately gather it back;
Unify it in one place, and nothing is not accomplished.
The following is the instruction of the Fourth Patriarch of the Chan school, Master Daoxin, in
the Essential Expedient Method for Entering the Way and Settling the Mind

, on “guarding the one without moving.” Its method is simple, concrete, practical, and safe (it will not go astray); it is the fundamental practice for entering the Way — unify the mind in one place, and nothing is not accomplished.

Note: the translations within the annotations, for easier reading and understanding, are also set off with quotation marks, but what is within the quotation marks is not the original text; readers should note this.

[As for guarding the one without moving: with this empty, pure eye, attentively gaze upon one object, regardless of day or night, with single-minded precision constantly unmoving. If the mind is about to scatter, hastily gather it back, as with a rope tied to a bird's foot that, about to fly, is yanked back
chè
again. Gazing without ceasing all day long, [the mind] naturally settles in serene oneness.]

Guarding the one without moving means: with this empty, pure eye, attentively gaze upon one object, and whether day or night, with single-minded vigor and constancy, gaze without scattering and without drowsiness. If the mind (the attention) scatters, immediately gather it back — just as a bird's foot is tied with a rope, and when the bird is about to fly away it is immediately yanked back. Day after day, from morning to evening, continually gazing thus and continually gathering back the runaway mind, as time passes and the practice matures, one reaches the state in which deluded thoughts vanish completely (serene oneness), and the mind naturally settles down.
[Guarding the one without moving]The mind (the attention) guards one place and does not move away. The Sixth Patriarch said:
“I announce to all who study the Way: strive, and you must apply your mind.”

(The Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch.) [Empty, pure eye]“Empty, pure eye” means: seeing is only seeing, like a mirror reflecting objects — seeing without thinking. [Attentively gaze upon one object]One object is just one thing. For example, you may set up a ping-pong ball and gaze upon it. (To place it easily, you can stick the ping-pong ball onto a small piece of cardboard.) When the practice matures, you may choose according to different circumstances — for example, a single leaf, a teacup, and so on; anywhere is a place to practice. [With single-minded precision constantly unmoving]“Unmoving” here means the attention does not move away, that is, non-scattering and non-drowsiness. [If the mind is about to scatter]If deluded thoughts arise, it shows that the gazing is not focused, not continuous, or even that one has forgotten to gaze. At such a time, gather your spirits and gaze focused and continuously. If you truly gaze focused and continuously, deluded thoughts will naturally cease. Of course, to be able to gaze focused and continuously — even focused, continuous, and sustained — requires a process of nurturing and training, and this is the practice. The key is “gazing without ceasing all day long”; the skill is trained in just this way. For a beginner, the mind keeps running off and one keeps gathering it back; though the whole hour is a tug-of-war, you have still made full use of that hour. [Serene oneness]This is used to describe the scene of miscellaneous thoughts vanishing completely.
[As with a rope tied to a bird's foot, about to fly, is yanked back]The bird's foot-rope here is also like the ox-nose rope of which the Chan school later spoke.
The Great Master Dahui said:
Since you have studied this Way
(investigating Chan)
, in the twelve hours, wherever you meet things and respond to conditions, do not let evil thoughts
(for
a cultivator of the Way
, deluded thoughts are evil thoughts, because they cut off the Dharma-body and wisdom-life)
continue. Or if you fail to attend and an evil thought arises, you should at once gather your spirits
(immediately
rouse yourself
and turn your head back
turning from deluded thought back to right thought
. If you always
(always)
follow it, continuing without break, not only does it obstruct the Way, but this is also called a person without wisdom. Of old, Weishan asked Lan'an
(the Chan Master Da'an)
: ‘In the twelve hours, what is your business?
(In the twenty-four hours, what are you doing?)
An said: ‘Herding the ox.’ Shan said: ‘How do you herd it?
(How do you herd?)
An said: ‘Once it goes into the grass
(deluded thoughts arising)
, I yank it back by the nose.
(As soon as the ox leaves the right path, I pull hard on the nose-rope and bring it back.)
Shan said: ‘You
(you)
truly herd the ox!
(You truly are herding the mind-ox!)
One who studies the Way and restrains evil thoughts
restraining
deluded thoughts)
should be like Lan'an herding the ox; then in time it will naturally become thoroughly familiar
(deluded thoughts not arising)
(The Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Dahui Pujue.)

With this empty, pure eye, attentively gaze upon one object, regardless of day or night, with single-minded precision constantly unmoving. If the mind is about to scatter, hastily gather it back, as with a rope tied to a bird's foot that, about to fly, is yanked back again. Gazing without ceasing all day long, [the mind] naturally settles in serene oneness.”
These ten lines are the verse-secret of guarding the one without moving,
extremely exquisite

. Those who study it must hold them firmly in mind, reciting them constantly, savoring them constantly, and putting them into practice constantly. When the skill matures, with a single gaze deluded thoughts are cut off on the spot — this is the great method of ending birth and death.

[The Vimalakirti Sutra says: “Gathering the mind is the bodhimanda.” This is the method of gathering the mind. The Lotus Sutra says: “For countless kalpas, apart from sleep, always gather the mind; through these various merits, one is able to produce the various concentrations.” The Sutra of the Buddha's Bequeathed Teaching says: “Of the five sense-roots, the mind is their master.
Unify it in one place, and nothing is not accomplished.” This is it.]
The Vimalakirti Sutra says:

“Gathering the mind is the bodhimanda.” This “guarding the one without moving (like a rope tied to a bird's foot, about to fly, is yanked back)” is precisely the method of gathering the mind. The Lotus Sutra says: “The bodhisattva, in his practice, for countless kalpas, apart from sleep, is constantly gathering the mind; because of the merit of gathering the mind, he is able to produce the concentrations.” The Sutra of the Buddha's Bequeathed Teaching says: “The eye, ear, nose, tongue, and body — these five roots — the mind is their master.

Unify the mind in one place, then nothing is not accomplished.” This “guarding the one without moving” is the “method of gathering the mind,” is “constantly gathering the mind,” is “unify it in one place and nothing is not accomplished”!

[Gathering the mind]To gather the mind into one place. [Gathering the mind is the bodhimanda]As long as one can gather the mind, there is no place that is not a bodhimanda. [Apart from sleep, always gather the mind]The Lotus Sutra says:

“Again, for countless kalpas, dwelling in empty and secluded places, whether sitting or walking in meditation, apart from sleep, always gathering the mind; because of this causal condition, one is able to produce the various concentrations.”
[Able to produce the various concentrations]Able to produce the concentrations. Here “various” (zhu) is a preposition, equivalent to “in/among.”
Question: Before falling asleep one is in a state of closed eyes. How does one do the practice of guarding the one without moving?

Answer: You may “observe the light.” The method is: whether sitting or lying, close your eyes and fix the attention gazing straight ahead (if lying down, then gaze upward). If the mind scatters, immediately gather it back. After a while, a cloud of light or a point of light may appear; at that time, attentively gaze upon the cloud of light or point of light. But do not cling to it; it is merely “one object” of “attentively gazing upon one object.” Though the eyes are closed, one is still seeing with the “empty, pure eye” — seeing without thinking. If there is no cloud or point of light, it is enough to know that you are gazing straight ahead. The important thing is:
If the mind scatters, immediately gather it back.
Alternatively, you may also inwardly gaze upon the dantian, guarding it with the mind.
The key point remains:
If the mind scatters, immediately gather it back.

[Dantian]Here it refers to the lower dantian, which is the Guanyuan point of the Conception Vessel, located three inches below the navel (about four finger-widths), and is the place where essence is stored. The lower dantian is the main place for training, gathering, and storing genuine qi. A person's primal qi originates in the kidneys, is stored in the dantian, and, through the pathway of the three burners, circulates throughout the whole body, thereby driving the functional activities of the five viscera and six bowels. The strength or weakness of the body, and life and death, all depend on the flourishing or decline of the dantian's primal qi; therefore, cultivating and protecting the dantian's primal qi is extremely important. When the dantian's primal qi is full and vigorous, it can mobilize the body's potential, enabling the genuine qi to circulate throughout the whole body. Guarding the dantian with the mind can regulate yin and yang, connect the heart and kidneys, make the genuine qi full and unobstructed through the eight vessels, restore the innate physiological functions, and promote health and longevity.

blocks.text: Appendix: Unifying the Mind in One Place

inline.s: (Recorded from
the Commentary on the Sutra of the Buddha's Bequeathed Teaching

[These five sense-roots — the mind is their master; therefore you should well restrain the mind. The fearfulness of the mind is greater than that of a venomous snake, a fierce beast, or a hostile robber; even a raging great fire is not sufficient to compare with it. It is like a person who holds a vessel of honey, moving about lightly and restlessly, only gazing at the honey, not seeing the deep pit before him. It is like a mad elephant without a hook, or a monkey that has gotten into a tree, leaping and bounding, difficult to restrain. You should quickly subdue it, not letting it be lax. To indulge this mind loses a person's good deeds; unify it in one place, and nothing is not accomplished. Therefore, bhikshus, you should be diligent and vigorous and subdue your minds.]

These five sense-roots (eye, ear, nose, tongue, body) — the mind is their master; therefore you must well control your own mind. The fearfulness of a scattered mind is greater than that of a venomous snake, a fierce beast, or a hostile robber; even a sky-filling great fire is not as fearful as it. This is like a person carrying a bowl of honey, complacently only looking at the honey in the bowl, not seeing the deep pit before him. Again it is like a mad elephant without an iron hook to control it, racing wildly away; and like a monkey that has gotten into a forest, leaping and bounding, difficult to restrain. As soon as the mind is the least bit scattered, you should immediately subdue it (gather it back), not letting it be lax. To indulge this mind loses a person's good deeds; unify the mind in one place, then nothing is not accomplished. Therefore, bhikshus, you should be diligent and vigorous and tame your minds.
This is to say: the mind is the master of the five sense-roots and directs the five sense-roots; therefore, if one wishes to restrain the five sense-roots, one must first restrain the mind.

[Should well restrain the mind]To make skill in restraining the mind. [A mad elephant without a hook]The “mad elephant” is a metaphor for the mind's mad delusion, and “without a hook” is a metaphor for losing control. The Nirvana Sutra says: “The mind is light, restless, and ever turning; hard to grasp, hard to tame. It races and runs wild, like a great evil elephant.” It also says: “It is like a drunken elephant, mad and stupid, vicious and evil, with a great desire to kill. There is an elephant-tamer who, with a great iron hook, hooks and strikes the top of its head, and instantly it is trained and submissive, with all its evil mind gone. All sentient beings likewise are thus.” [The word is,
ái

]meaning foolish. [Good deeds]The wholesome dharmas of humans and heavens and the wholesome dharmas that transcend the world are collectively called good deeds. [Subdue your mind]This says: the mind is a servant, not to be indulged, and still less to be allowed to be master; rather, one oneself should be master of the mind and ride the mind. Therefore practice is cultivating the mind — taming the mind, which is the practice of herding the ox.
